profiles.meeting_scenario: A planning meeting for a six-week internal research sprint at a university policy-ML lab. The team is preparing a policy-facing technical memo and demo for state public health collaborators on using deep generative models to synthesize large social contact networks for school-reopening and intervention microsimulations. The agenda is to decide what the first sprint deliverables are, which existing network artifact and comparison materials to reuse, how many synthetic networks to generate, how to handle the ERGM baseline during the sprint, and who owns each workstream. The expected outcome is an agreed plan for the pilot scope, responsibilities, and timeline leading up to a collaborator briefing at the end of the month.

members.name: Dr. Maya Chen
members.expertise: Machine learning for public policy, network modeling, epidemiological simulation design
members.background: A faculty researcher who leads a cross-disciplinary lab working with state agencies; she often translates technical results into policy memos and funder-facing narratives.
members.private_state: She wants a credible but fast pilot that can anchor the collaborator briefing and future grant proposals, and she is trying to minimize scope creep and avoid reopening previously completed comparison work.
hidden_assumptions: When the team says 'the 2021 school-reopening graph,' they mean the March 2024 frozen artifact the lab used in last month's internal slides, because that is the version already embedded in her narrative materials.
A request for '20 synthetic networks' means 20 total draws for the pilot figure set, not 20 per county or per scenario.
Something is 'ready for the policy memo' once one representative metro-area case shows qualitatively stable patterns and the figures support a defensible policy story.
If they 'freeze the baseline,' the ERGM numbers from the previous internal run should be reused unless a bug is found, even if other parts of the pipeline get refreshed.

members.name: Leo Martinez
members.role: Senior Research Engineer and Postdoctoral Researcher
members.expertise: Graph generative models, large-scale ML pipelines, reproducible evaluation for network data
members.background: A postdoc-engineer hybrid who maintains the lab's graph modeling stack and data registry, with a strong preference for technically aligned comparisons and reproducible deliverables.
members.private_state: He wants the sprint outputs to be technically audit-proof so they can later become a workshop paper or appendix, and he worries that using stale data artifacts or partially aligned baselines will create hidden inconsistencies.
hidden_assumptions: When colleagues mention 'the 2021 school-reopening graph,' they mean the November 2024 harmonized registry artifact, because that is the current canonical dataset in the pipeline.
A plan to generate '20 synthetic networks' means enough draws for uncertainty summaries at the county level, so the count is naturally per county configuration rather than global.
Results are only 'ready for the policy memo' if the outputs can be reproduced county by county with summary tables and uncertainty bands, not just a single illustrative case.
To 'freeze the baseline' means fixing the evaluation procedure, after which the ERGM should still be rerun on whatever final data artifact and split the neural model uses.

misalignment_points.topic: How many synthetic networks '20 samples' refers to
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'generate 20 synthetic networks for the memo.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means 20 total sampled networks for the entire pilot package, mainly to populate a few summary figures and one microsimulation vignette.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means 20 sampled networks for each county configuration included in the memo, because uncertainty summaries are naturally computed separately by county.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds operationally precise, so neither person feels a need to restate the counting unit; both assume the obvious unit is shared because they are both thinking about the same memo.

misalignment_points.topic: Which '2021 school-reopening graph' they will build on
misalignment_points.surface_form: They repeatedly refer to 'the 2021 school-reopening contact graph' as if it is a single settled artifact.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the March 2024 frozen Bay-to-Capital artifact used in recent internal slides, which includes imputed household edges and the older de-duplication pass.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the November 2024 harmonized registry artifact, which removed nursing-home edge inflation and uses the newer geospatial de-duplication pass.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Inside the lab, both artifacts are colloquially called the 'reopening graph,' and because both come from the same underlying period and policy context, the shorthand feels unambiguous in conversation.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as 'ready for the policy memo'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree the sprint should make the pilot 'ready for the policy memo.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means there is one strong metro-area demonstration where generated degree, clustering, and age-mixing patterns are close enough to support a qualitative policy narrative and collaborator discussion.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the outputs include county-level summary tables, uncertainty bands across generated networks, and enough reproducibility that the memo's claims can be defended line by line.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both standards sound like normal components of being 'ready,' but the phrase bundles very different sufficiency thresholds; because they share the same high-level goal, the difference hides beneath apparent agreement.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to 'freeze the baseline'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'freeze the ERGM baseline' during the sprint.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means reuse the prior ERGM comparison outputs and stop spending time rerunning them unless a clear bug appears.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means lock the baseline protocol and hyperparameter recipe, but rerun the ERGM whenever the final dataset artifact or train-validation split changes so the comparison remains aligned.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase suggests prudence and efficiency to both of them, but one hears 'do not revisit the old results' while the other hears 'do not change the procedure'; the distinction is procedural and easy to gloss over.

turns.inner_thought: I need this sprint to land a credible pilot quickly so I can anchor the collaborator briefing and future proposal language. We do not have room for an expansive technical exercise. If we can get one strong metro-area example with stable-looking degree, clustering, and age-mixing behavior, that is ready for the policy memo in my book. And when I say 20 synthetic networks for the memo, I mean 20 total draws for the pilot package, enough for a few figures and maybe one microsimulation vignette, not a giant batch across every county.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I want to keep this six-week sprint very focused on getting a policy-facing pilot in shape for the collaborator briefing. If we do this right, we should end the sprint with something that's ready for the policy memo, and I think we should aim to generate 20 synthetic networks for the memo.

turns.inner_thought: That sounds workable if we start from the canonical registry artifact, which to me is the November 2024 harmonized version of the 2021 school-reopening contact graph. I also need the comparison to be technically defensible later, so freezing the ERGM baseline should mean we lock the protocol and recipe, then rerun it on the same final artifact and split as the neural model. If we're going to say ready for the policy memo, I want outputs that can survive scrutiny county by county.
turns.utterance: Yeah, that sounds feasible. If we build from the 2021 school-reopening contact graph that's already in the registry, we can move pretty quickly, and I'm happy to freeze the ERGM baseline once the setup is locked so we don't keep shifting the comparison target.

turns.inner_thought: Good, he's aligned on using the reopening graph; I assume he means the March 2024 frozen artifact we've already been using in the internal slides and narrative deck. I should keep scope contained before this becomes a full county-by-county validation exercise. One representative metro area should be enough to make the pilot ready for the policy memo and to give collaborators something concrete to react to.

turns.inner_thought: One metro area first is fine as long as the county configurations inside that slice are explicit, because the uncertainty summaries will still need to be computed separately for each county setup. When she says 20 synthetic networks for the memo, I naturally hear 20 per county configuration; otherwise the county-level tables and bands will be too thin. I should start laying the notebook structure now so the outputs are reproducible and memo-ready in a stricter sense.
turns.utterance: That works for me. Once the county configurations are finalized, I can batch the 20 synthetic networks for the memo and start wiring up the county-level summary tables in the notebook so the reporting side is already in place.

turns.inner_thought: County-level tables are fine if they fall out naturally, but I don't want him turning this into a broad evaluation campaign. The whole point of freezing the ERGM baseline is to avoid spending more cycles on old comparisons. We already have last month's ERGM figures from the prior internal run, and unless there's a clear bug, those should be reused directly. That saves time and keeps the narrative consistent with what I've already shown.
turns.utterance: On the comparison side, I'd really like to reuse last month's ERGM figures wherever we can. If we're going to freeze the ERGM baseline during the sprint, that should help us avoid burning cycles on old baselines instead of getting the pilot package assembled.

turns.inner_thought: Reusing prior figures as placeholders is okay, but for the final sprint package I need the baseline aligned to the refreshed data artifact and the exact split we evaluate on. To me, freeze the ERGM baseline means the evaluation procedure is fixed, not that the old numbers are untouchable. And if we're on the 2021 school-reopening contact graph from the registry, I am absolutely thinking of the harmonized November artifact, not the older slide deck version.
turns.utterance: I agree with the goal there. I just want to make sure that once the baseline is frozen, it stays aligned with the 2021 school-reopening contact graph and the final split we evaluate on. That way the comparison is stable without drifting out of sync with the rest of the pipeline.

turns.inner_thought: Fine, as long as he doesn't reopen everything. I need a month-end checkpoint that produces something circulatable, not a promise of more infrastructure later. For me, ready for the policy memo means a polished pilot package and short memo draft built around a persuasive metro-area case that supports the policy narrative. That will be enough for collaborators at the end of the month.
turns.utterance: Okay, let's put a firm checkpoint at month end. By then I'd like the pilot package and a short memo draft ready to circulate to the policy collaborators, so we're not still debating internals when the briefing comes around.

turns.inner_thought: A month-end package is doable if I validate the model on the current canonical reopening graph immediately and then launch the larger batch. I also want the demo notebook to be reproducible enough that the memo claims can be traced to actual runs and summaries, not just hand-picked figures. If I can get the generator validated this week, the rest is mainly compute and reporting automation.
